comments.author: Ankita Gulati
comments.comment:
The real separator is not “built an agent”, it is “measured the agent.”

A fresher who can show task success rate, failure modes, latency, cost per run, and what changed after evals will stand out fast. Most projects stop at a demo video, production work starts when the model fails and you can explain why.

What eval would you expect a junior AI engineer to include in their first project? #AgenticAI

comments.author: Jaya Kishore Reddy Gollareddy
comments.comment: The hard part with multi-LLM routing is not picking the best model once, it is keeping the router calibrated as model quality, latency, and pricing shift every few weeks. I’d be curious how teams are measuring routing quality beyond task success, especially for voice where latency and interruption handling can matter as much as answer accuracy.

comments.author: Tim Oudeman
comments.comment: The hardest part of personal agent setups is usually not tool wiring, it is permission design. Read-only research, explicit approval gates, and per-agent memory boundaries are what keep a useful assistant from becoming an unpredictable automation layer. How are you planning to evaluate whether the agents are improving over time versus just accumulating more context?

comments.author: Narendra Cherlopalli
comments.comment: A production-ready agent should have an access contract before it has a demo: exact systems, exact actions, exact approval path, exact rollback owner. The failure mode I see most often is not model quality, it is a pilot with temporary permissions that nobody revisits once users start depending on it.

comments.author: Sumanth P
comments.comment: The hard part is not routing tasks between agents, it is making identity, memory, permissions, and auditability boring enough that teams can trust the system. Once agents move from personal assistant to shared infra, evals also need to shift from “did it answer well?” to “did it act correctly under the right scope?”
